content: The functioning of a trauma center has been shown to improve the process of medical care, with fewer deficiencies noted after a review process. This improvement is also evidenced by a reduction in mortality rates among severely injured patients. Verification of trauma centers has been identified as a critical component in the development of trauma management systems. Adapting the trauma center verification process to align with efforts to promote the Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care would conceptually mirror the processes used in high-income countries. However, significant modifications would be necessary to accommodate the existing systems of hospital accreditation, management, and supervision in a given country. For instance, criteria from the Essential Trauma Care (EsTC) guidelines, particularly those of high importance, could be integrated into existing review processes. Alternatively, specific reviews of trauma treatment facilities might be appropriate for hospitals managing large numbers of trauma patients. The integration of trauma management systems requires planning for pre-hospital emergency medical services (EMS), pre-hospital triage, transfer criteria, and inter-hospital transfer arrangements. Pre-hospital triage systems, especially in areas with well-organized EMS and multiple hospitals with varying trauma capabilities, aim to ensure that severely injured patients are transported to the most suitable hospital, not necessarily the geographically closest one. This involves bypassing less-equipped hospitals in favor of better-equipped facilities, provided the transport time is reasonable. EMS personnel are trained in triage criteria, including scoring algorithms like the trauma score and pre-hospital index. This also necessitates pre-existing arrangements between EMS and hospitals within a specific area. The designation of trauma centers involves selecting hospitals expected to meet varying levels of trauma capability, ranging from small rural hospitals to large urban trauma centers. This process is distinct from verification and is often accompanied by inter-hospital transfer agreements and protocols. These agreements aim to reduce transfer times, minimize complications during transport, and optimize care at both ends of the transfer through effective communication between medical providers. While such formal arrangements are more common in high-income countries, informal systems often exist in other settings to assess which cases require referral to larger facilities. Communication and transport are essential components of trauma management systems. Communication includes radio links between EMS units and receiving hospitals, allowing for prior notification and preparation for the arrival of severely injured patients. Designated telephone numbers and assigned tasks facilitate inter-hospital transfers. Transport arrangements for inter-facility transfers are also critical, though barriers such as patient or family preferences, costs, and logistical limitations often exist. In low-income settings, transport is frequently arranged by relatives using private or commercial vehicles, highlighting the economic barriers to formal EMS systems. Addressing these barriers could be part of a broader trauma management plan. In settings without formal EMS, principles of trauma care organization still apply. For example, in Ghana, a pilot program trained commercial drivers in basic first aid, as they were already transporting most severely injured patients to hospitals. This program demonstrated improvements in basic first-aid maneuvers, including triage. The siting of trauma care facilities should consider geographic distribution and need. Hospitals with high trauma volumes, such as those staffed by general practitioners along major roadways, could be targeted for improvements to meet minimum criteria for essential trauma care. Data collection and injury surveillance are crucial for ongoing evaluation and improvement of trauma management systems. Accurate data on injuries and related deaths are necessary to assess needs and monitor progress. Efforts to improve trauma care systems require interaction and coordination among stakeholders, including ministries of health, professional societies, WHO offices, and community groups. These stakeholders can develop plans for implementing the Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care, leading to widespread, low-cost improvements or pilot projects with appropriate research and evaluation. National governments must enhance their capacity to upgrade trauma services, often through a central agency representing all stakeholders. This agency should build consensus on the guidelines, accommodate local innovations, and ensure smooth coordination across all phases of trauma care, from pre-hospital to rehabilitation. The success of essential trauma care programs depends on grassroots implementation, integration into national policies, and continuous monitoring and evaluation. National, provincial, and local mandates may be necessary to support these efforts. The guidelines serve as a flexible template to assist with planning and catalyze improvements in trauma management systems. Progress has already been made in some countries, such as Mexico and India, where local adaptations of the guidelines have been implemented through collaboration among various stakeholders. These examples demonstrate the intended use of the guidelines to improve trauma care systems globally.
